method: A rectilinear lens spreads the sensor's horizontal pixels across a scene that widens with distance, so the scene width at distance d is 2 x d x tan(HFOV / 2) and the pixel density is the frame width divided by that width, in pixels per metre. Doubling the distance halves the density; halving it doubles the density. Square pixels make the vertical density identical, which is why only the horizontal field of view is asked for: the vertical field of view is 2 x atan(tan(HFOV / 2) x height / width) and height / scene height gives the same number. The IEC 62676-4:2014 operational requirements are 25 px/m for detection, 62.5 px/m for observation, 125 px/m for recognition and 250 px/m for identification (published as 25, 63, 125 and 250 px/m, or 8, 20, 40 and 80 px/ft); identification works out at 40 pixels across a 0.16 m human face, and the page reports the pixels on that face. A level is met when the density is greater than or equal to its threshold, so a distance exactly at a level's limit still counts for that level. The reach of a level is width / (2 x tan(HFOV / 2) x threshold) - where that division lands on the threshold - and the pixels needed to identify a face at the entered distance is the scene width x 250, rounded up. Density in px/ft is px/m divided by 3.28084. The model assumes a rectilinear lens with square pixels and no distortion, a face square to the camera at the stated distance, even lighting and a sharp image; fisheye and panoramic lenses, tilted or receding faces, motion blur, low light, IR illumination and compression all reduce the effective density, so this is a planning guide rather than a guarantee. IEC 62676-4:2025 replaced these four names with a seven-step scale, all of which this page does not model. Inputs are whole pixels from 16 to 32,768, a field of view strictly between 0 and 180 degrees and a distance from 0 to 10,000 m; there is no storage, upload or network access.
